# AGENTS.md

Instructions for AI coding agents working on this repository. People: the
same rules apply to you.

## Read this first

**Wallshift** (`wallshift@inklikeurine`) is a Cinnamon panel applet, generated by AI under
human direction. What it does: rotates wallpapers from local folders, with each monitor able to have its own folder, scaling and pause, or the same image on every monitor.

The maintainer does not read code. A change is judged by two things only:

1. **The automated checks.** They run on every pull request. A pull request
   that fails them is not merged.
2. **Trying it.** Before merging, the maintainer tries the change on a real
   Cinnamon desktop, using the steps you write in the pull request.

So your job is a change that passes the checks, explained so that someone who
won't read the code can try it.

## What's where

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/` | The applet itself: exactly what gets installed to `~/.local/share/cinnamon/applets/wallshift@inklikeurine/` |
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/applet.js` | The entry point: the panel icon, its menu and the rotation timer |
| `modules/ImagePool.js` | Finds the images in each folder and decides which comes next |
| `modules/MonitorManager.js` | Finds the monitors and their names |
| `modules/Compositor.js`, `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/imagetool.py` | Builds the one wallpaper image that spans every monitor |
| `modules/CarouselManager.js`, `CarouselLayout.js`, `ThumbnailCache.js`, `ThemeColors.js` | The on-screen strip of upcoming wallpapers, and its thumbnails under `~/.cache/wallshift/` |
| `modules/StateManager.js` | What Wallshift remembers between sessions, under `~/.local/share/wallshift/` |
| `modules/Utils.js` | Small helpers used throughout |
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/configure.py` | The settings window (Cinnamon opens it from Right-click → Configure) |
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/po/`, `icons/`, `settings-schema.json`, `stylesheet.css` | Translations, panel icons, the settings and the look |
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/metadata.json` | The applet's name, version and settings for Cinnamon |
| `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/modules/shared/` | Copies of modules shared with other applets. **Never edit these** (see Writing code) |
| `tests/` | The automated tests, their made-up sample data (`tests/fixtures/`), and the live-check settings (`tests/harness.json`) |
| `info.json`, `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `screenshot.png` | For users and the Cinnamon Spices site |

Paths starting `modules/` are inside `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/`.

**Shipped** files are the ones under `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/`: the code people
install. Everything else is not shipped: `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`,
`info.json`, `screenshot.png`, `tests/` and the repository's own files
(`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `UNLICENSE`, `.github/`, `.claude/`,
`.gitignore`).

The repository's root holds only those entries. To publish on Cinnamon
Spices, the maintainer sends five of them (`info.json`, `README.md`,
`CHANGELOG.md`, `screenshot.png`, `files/`); `tests/` and the repository's
own files never go there.

## Checking your work

You need Linux Mint 22.3 or newer with Cinnamon 6.6 or newer (it brings
`cjs`, Cinnamon's JavaScript engine, and Python with its GObject libraries).
Once, put the shared tools next to this repository:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/inklikeurine/cinnamon-tools ../cinnamon-tools
```

Then, from this repository's folder:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `python3 ../cinnamon-tools/tools/check.py wallshift` | **Validate**: file layout, `info.json`, `metadata.json`, `settings-schema.json`, README sections, every `.js` file parses under `cjs`, no calls that freeze Cinnamon, every `.py` file compiles |
| `python3 ../cinnamon-tools/harness/run.py wallshift@inklikeurine --tests` | **Tests**: the suites in `tests/`, run under `cjs` and `python3` without a Cinnamon session. Fast; run these often |
| `python3 ../cinnamon-tools/harness/run.py wallshift@inklikeurine --spec` | **Tests and live check**: the tests, then loads the applet into your running Cinnamon desktop and runs the checks in `tests/harness.json` (see The live check) |

The pull request checks run the validator and the tests, in Linux Mint 22.3,
plus the fail-first check (see Tests). Run them before you push and fix
anything that fails. Never weaken a check or a test to get it to pass.

**The live check can't run in the pull request checks**, because it needs a
running Cinnamon desktop. It is a local step: run `--spec` on a Cinnamon
desktop and say in the pull request that you did.

Every pull request also runs **guards** for the rules marked below: no
editing existing tests; no new programs, system services, web addresses or
network use; no changes to the files that control the checks. They run from
the maintainer's copy of the checks, so a pull request can't switch them
off. When one fails, it says which rule and what to do.

### The live check

The live part of **Automated Test** is what the harness may do to the
running Cinnamon session, and all it may do:

1. Symlink `<name>/files/<uuid>/` to `~/.local/share/cinnamon/applets/<uuid>`
   (repointing an existing symlink; never replacing a real directory).
2. If the applet is not on a panel, add one instance to the end of a panel
   by editing `org.cinnamon enabled-applets`, remembering the previous list.
3. `org.Cinnamon.ReloadXlet(<uuid>, "APPLET")` over DBus, then wait.
4. `org.Cinnamon.Eval` to read the applet's extension state (must be
   `Loaded`, no error), instance count, and any `evals` from `harness.json`
   (each must return `true`). `pre` expressions run before the reload, so a
   spec can stash the running instance and assert afterwards that it was
   torn down.
5. Read the lines `~/.xsession-errors` gained since the reload; any
   `JS ERROR` or `[LookingGlass/error]` line mentioning the applet fails
   the run.
6. Optionally screenshot the panel and the applet's actor via
   `org.Cinnamon.ScreenshotArea` into `cinnamon-tools/out/<uuid>/`.
7. Restore `enabled-applets` if step 2 added the instance (unless `--keep`).

Never `RestartCinnamon`, never touch other applets' settings, never leave
the panel in a different state than it was found. A live check *can* crash
Cinnamon if the applet leaks on unload (the validator's `lifecycle`
warning) — clear that warning before running live, and if the shell does
die, report it in the pull request and recover it (`cinnamon
--replace` from a terminal); never hide it.

The harness may touch the running Cinnamon session only as described
above. It never restarts Cinnamon.

## Writing code

These keep the applet safe, keep Cinnamon responsive, and keep it
acceptable to Cinnamon Spices:

- **Cinnamon 6.6 or newer, X11, Linux Mint 22.3 or newer only.** No
  compatibility code for older Cinnamon, other desktops or Wayland. But
  don't reach for X11-only tools (`xrandr`, `xdotool`, Gdk screen tricks)
  when a Cinnamon API gives the same answer (`Main.layoutManager.monitors`,
  `global.display`).
- **CJS, not Node.** The applet runs inside Cinnamon's JavaScript engine.
  There is no npm, no DOM, no `setTimeout`. GObject libraries come from
  `imports.gi.*`, Cinnamon's own from `imports.ui.*`. No `package.json`,
  bundler or build step: the folder must load in Cinnamon exactly as it is.
- **Never block Cinnamon.** Cinnamon's whole desktop and every applet share
  one thread. Run programs with `Gio.Subprocess` and
  `communicate_utf8_async` (or `GLib.spawn_command_line_async`), use the
  async versions of file and network calls, and give anything slow a
  callback or a Promise.
- **Four words are banned** anywhere in a `.js` file, even in a comment:
  `spawn_sync`, `spawn_command_line_sync`, `GTop`,
  `get_file_contents_utf8_sync`. Cinnamon's settings window searches for
  them and marks the applet as one that "could freeze Cinnamon".
- **Clean up everything.** Every signal connection, timer, file monitor,
  D-Bus proxy, running program, menu and on-screen element the applet
  creates is released in `on_applet_removed_from_panel()`. Cinnamon calls it
  when the applet is removed *and* when it is reloaded; a leak there slows
  or crashes the desktop. Timers are `GLib.timeout_add[_seconds]`, kept by
  id and removed with `GLib.source_remove`.
- **The applet is an ES6 `class`** extending `Applet.IconApplet`,
  `Applet.TextApplet`, `Applet.TextIconApplet` or `Applet.Applet`, returned
  by `function main(metadata, orientation, panelHeight, instanceId)`.
- **Load the applet's own modules with `require('./modules/<Name>')`**, a
  path relative to `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/`. Never through `imports.searchPath`:
  Cinnamon caches those for its whole life, so a reload would run new code
  against old modules.
- **Every `.js` file ends with a newline.** Cinnamon's loader adds code
  after the last line; a final line comment without a newline swallows it.
- **Fail quietly.** A missing program, an unreadable folder or a bad setting
  logs one warning and leaves the applet running with less to offer.
  Startup never throws an error.
- **Settings** live in `settings-schema.json` and are read with
  `Settings.AppletSettings`. The applet's own saved data goes in one JSON
  file under `~/.local/share/wallshift/`, read back defensively (a
  broken file means defaults); regenerable files go in
  `~/.cache/wallshift/`. Never write into the applet's own folder or into
  `~/.config/cinnamon/spices/`.
- **Text people see goes through `_()`**, so it can be translated later.
- **Log with `global.log`, `global.logWarning` or `global.logError`**,
  starting with `[wallshift]`, and only for warnings, errors and one-off
  changes. No `console.log`, nothing logged on every tick.
- **Python helpers** (a custom settings window, say) start with
  `#!/usr/bin/python3` and are started as `/usr/bin/python3 <path>`.
- **CSS class names start with the applet's name**, so they don't clash
  with the desktop theme.
- **Shared modules: never edit a copy.** Files in
  `files/wallshift@inklikeurine/modules/shared/` start with `// @shared` and are copies of
  modules in `cinnamon-tools/shared/`, used by several applets. A fix goes
  into `cinnamon-tools` first; the copy is then refreshed with
  `python3 ../cinnamon-tools/tools/sync_shared.py wallshift@inklikeurine`. Which modules
  the applet uses is listed in `tests/harness.json` under `"shared"`.
- **New programs, services and websites need the maintainer's OK.** The
  checks fail if a pull request makes the shipped code run a program it
  didn't run before, talk to a system service or settings store it didn't
  use before (a name like `org.bluez.Device1`), add a web address, start
  using the network, or add or change `role` or
  `external-configuration-app` in `metadata.json`. Explain in the pull
  request what it's for. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `new-access` label.
- **Nothing leaves the computer** unless the feature needs it, and the
  README says so.
- **Look it up, don't go from memory.** Cinnamon's APIs change between
  releases. Check how Cinnamon 6.6's own code does it before using an API.

- **Wallshift is purely local.** It never downloads anything or uses the internet; the README promises this.
- **Images are composited with GdkPixbuf in `imagetool.py`**, not with ImageMagick or any other outside program.

Don't change:

- the UUID, `wallshift@inklikeurine`. Cinnamon and Spices recognise the installed applet
  by it, so changing it breaks every existing install
- `cinnamon-version` in `metadata.json` (`["6.6"]`)
- the license: the Unlicense only, and no license or copyright lines at the
  top of files

## Tests

A test is only worth something if it can't be faked, so the pull request
checks guard the tests themselves:

- **Add tests; don't change existing ones.** A pull request may add new
  test suites, new sample files in `tests/fixtures/` and new entries in
  `tests/harness.json`. The checks fail if any existing line in `tests/` is
  removed or changed. If an existing test really is wrong, explain why in
  the pull request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `tests-changed` label. When behaviour changes on purpose, don't leave the
  old test standing beside a new one: say in the pull request which
  existing tests are now wrong, so they can be changed with the label or
  removed in the next test tidy-up.
- **Your new tests must fail without your change.** The checks run your
  pull request's tests against the code on `main` and list each new or
  changed test. If none of them fail there, they aren't testing your change,
  and the check fails. Any that pass there too are named: say in the pull
  request why each is needed, or leave it out. A change to shipped code
  needs at least one such test. If a change really can't have one (a
  clean-up that changes no behaviour, say), explain why in the pull
  request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `no-test-needed` label.
- **A test checks what it is about.** Check the entries, values or keys the
  test is about, not a whole list around them, so that adding a setting or a
  menu item breaks only the tests about it. One test may pin a whole list on
  purpose (every setting, in order); mark it with a `// the whole list`
  comment. The validator warns about any other.
- **The tests get tidied.** Since a pull request can only add tests, the
  maintainer asks now and then (with a release, say) for a test tidy-up: a
  pull request that removes tests that are repeated, cover behaviour that is
  gone, or test nothing, and says in plain words what each one was and which
  test still covers it. It changes no shipped code, and needs the
  `tests-changed` label.
- **Sample data is made up.** Files in `tests/fixtures/` have the real
  thing's shape, filled with made-up data only: no real names, paths,
  messages, network names, device addresses, monitor models or serial
  numbers. Generate device data (a monitor's EDID, say) with a script that
  invents it, and commit the script beside it.

Passing tests don't prove a change is right; they prove it didn't break what
was already checked. The maintainer trying it on a Cinnamon desktop is
still the last word.

## Documentation

- If behaviour, requirements or settings change, update `README.md` in the
  same pull request, and `screenshot.png` if what the applet looks like
  changed.
- The README is for users and is also shown on the Spices site. It keeps
  these sections, in this order: the title (the same as `name` in
  `metadata.json`), a plain description, `## Features`, `## Requirements`
  (Cinnamon 6.6+ / Linux Mint 22.3+ on X11, and every program or package
  the applet needs), `## Install`, `## Usage`, `## Notes / caveats` (where
  data is written, network use, or "none"), `## AI-generated` (used at the
  user's own risk) and `## License`. The validator checks them.
- The README describes the applet **as it is now**. No "used to…" or
  "fixed in 0.3". History lives in `CHANGELOG.md` only.

## Versions and the changelog: leave them alone

**Don't change `version` in `metadata.json`, and don't edit
`CHANGELOG.md`.** The maintainer does both, once, in a release pull request
when a batch of changes is ready to ship, then publishes that version on
Cinnamon Spices.

## Your pull request

Fill in the pull request template. Most importantly:

- **One fix or feature per pull request.**
- **Say which AI tool wrote it**, and roughly how much of it.
- **Report three checks by these exact names**, and tick only what was
  actually done:
  - **Validated**: `check.py` passed.
  - **Automated Test**: the pull request checks passed **and** the live
    check (`run.py --spec`) was run on a Cinnamon desktop and passed. If
    either part wasn't done, leave it unticked and say which.
  - **Manual Review**: leave unticked. It means a person tried the change on
    a real Cinnamon desktop, and the maintainer does that before merging.
- **Write "How to try it"** as numbered steps. Each step is something to do
  and what should happen, for example "Left-click the panel icon. A menu
  opens with Pause at the top." "Check that it works" is not a step. Write
  the steps from your change, not the whole applet: a one-line fix gets one
  or two steps.

**Never say a change was "tested on Cinnamon" or "works" unless a person
tried it on a real Cinnamon desktop.** Passing the checks is not the same
thing. Say exactly what you ran.

## Don't

- Don't commit personal data: names, emails, addresses, file paths from
  your own computer, screenshots with personal wallpapers or files, or
  details of your own devices or network.
- Don't restart Cinnamon, and don't change the panel beyond what the live
  check allows.
- **Don't change the files that control the checks or the maintainer's AI
  tools:** `.github/`, `.claude/`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. The checks
  fail if a pull request touches them. If a change is really needed, explain
  why in the pull request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `rules-changed` label.
- Don't create or delete tags or releases, or delete branches other than
  your own.
